name: Ndebele Kingdom (Mthwakazi)
summary: A kingdom founded by Mzilikazi, a former Zulu general, who settled north of the Limpopo in 1838; his son Lobengula ruled until the British South Africa Company conquered it in 1893–94.

knownFor.label: Rudd Concession
knownFor.note: Mining deal that opened the way to conquest.

location.value: Matabeleland, the west and south-west of Zimbabwe.

terrain.value: A high grassland plateau with granite hills such as the Matobo Hills, and river valleys.

climate.value: Dry savanna, with summer rains from about November to March and dry, cool winters.

resources.value: Good grazing for cattle, farmland for grain, and old gold workings that drew European prospectors.

disasters.value: Droughts and locusts that hurt crops; cattle diseases also caused losses.

population.value: About 3,435,000 Ndebele today (2023 estimate), 2,200,000 of them in Zimbabwe; the page gives no figure for the kingdom.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

economicBase.value: Cattle mattered: Lobengula’s warriors raided Shona cattle in 1893, and a year of drought and cattle sickness preceded the 1896 revolt; the page gives no other economic detail.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with traders and hunters from the south via the “Hunters’ Road”: ivory and cattle for guns, cloth and beads.

wealth.value: Wealth measured in cattle, much of it held by the king and given to regiments and chiefs.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: Mzilikazi organised a militaristic system of regimental towns with Bulawayo as capital; Lobengula held sovereignty over the region between the Limpopo and Zambezi rivers.

keyRulers.value: Mzilikazi (reigned from 1823; died 9 September 1868); his son Lobengula succeeded him.

succession.value: A son of the king succeeded; after Mzilikazi died in 1868, Lobengula was installed in 1870 after a dispute.

institutions.value: Regimental towns, izinduna chiefs, and the inxwala first-fruits ceremony that renewed the king’s power each year.

stability.value: Strong under Mzilikazi and Lobengula until the British South Africa Company invaded in 1893.

eliteConflict.value: A succession dispute after Mzilikazi died in 1868; regiments opposing Lobengula were defeated by 1872.

armyAndTech.value: Regiments with short stabbing spears and cowhide shields; rifles came later, including through the Rudd Concession.

majorWars.value: First Matabele War from August 1893 (Lobengula burned his capital and fled); the Matabele revolt of March 1896 ended in October 1897.

territoryChange.value: Moved north of the Limpopo in 1838 after defeat by Boers in the Transvaal in 1837.

alliancesRivals.value: Raided Shona communities for cattle and tribute, and clashed with the Ngwato (Tswana) to the south-west.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; its regimental system was its best-known innovation.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Allowed traders, hunters and missionaries in, such as at Inyati (1859), but guarded its land.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, messengers between regimental towns, and ox-wagon tracks from the south.

religion.value: Mlimo is named as the Ndebele spiritual leader; today most Ndebele are Christian with a minority following traditional religion.

languageWriting.value: isiNdebele, a Nguni language close to Zulu; no writing until missionaries began recording it.

artsArchitecture.value: Beadwork, praise poetry (izibongo), dance at the inxwala ceremony, and thatched homesteads with cattle pens.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king and to one’s regiment helped join people of different origins.

dailyLife.value: Homesteads with thatched huts and cattle pens; sorghum and millet porridge, beer and milk.

neighbours.value: Shona chiefdoms to the east, the Ngwato and other Tswana to the south-west, and the Boer Transvaal to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Sacred kingship: the inxwala ceremony each year confirmed the king’s link to ancestors and the land.

colonisation.value: Conquered by the British South Africa Company (1893).

riseSignals.value: Mzilikazi built three military strongholds between 1827 and 1832 and fought Boer trekkers in 1836–38; he then led about 20,000 Ndebele to western Zimbabwe, named the nation Mthwakazi, and made Bulawayo his capital.

peakPeriod.value: The page names no peak. It calls Lobengula the second and last king (1870–94); the kingdom was a significant power until British occupation, and it lost an estimated 600,000 cattle to dispossession.

declineSignals.value: The Rudd Concession of 1888 gave mineral rights to Cecil Rhodes’s agents, leading to the 1890 Pioneer Column.

outcome.value: Became part of Rhodesia; today Zimbabwe.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
